rows.body:
In this module, you'll learn how to use an AI chatbot (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Copilot), guided by a web app I built, to create and refine multiple-choice questions for nursing education. You will need access to an AI chatbot, but you don't need any kind of previous experience.

You'll work through short readings, videos, and ungraded knowledge checks, followed by a short period of guided practice. You can leave this module at any time; when you open it again, it will resume where you left off.

Because you teach in nursing education, you've probably seen your fair share of multiple-choice questions, and may have to regularly write some, too. In fact, when Birkhead and colleagues surveyed prelicensure nursing faculty about this, they found that nearly all of their respondents used standard multiple-choice questions.

rows.header: Writing good multiple-choice questions can be hard
rows.body: Unfortunately, even in high-stakes nursing exams, a large share of questions contain item-writing flaws. These flaws can make a question ineffective and unfair.
Below is a question with several item-writing flaws. Take a moment to look it over and see how many you can spot.

Here's the same question with the flaws annotated. While it's unusual to see a single question with this many flaws, you've likely seen each one of them at one point.

An important note on the scope of this module: I didn't design it to teach the principles of writing high-quality multiple-choice questions. For that, I recommend Vicki Moran's *Item Writing for Nurse Educators* (2023). I accessed it digitally through my institution's library at no extra cost, and yours may offer similar access: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30211-4

When Moran and colleagues surveyed nursing faculty about their exam writing, 31% said they were neutral or less confident in their ability to write exam items. 31% might not seem like a high number, but if you stop and think about what it represents across all of nursing education, it translates into a significant number of educators who could use support.

And it isn't only about competence; even for those who are confident, writing good multiple-choice questions can take a lot of time and effort, over and over, every exam cycle.
This video explains how high-quality multiple-choice questions support learning and why they remain important in nursing education.

rows.stem: Based on the video, which statement best describes retrieval practice?
rows.correct_blob: Pulling information from memory strengthens long-term learning more than rereading.
rows.distractors_blob:
Reviewing material several times in a row is the most reliable way to commit it to memory ||
Learning is strongest when students are exposed to information in as many formats as possible ||
To support long-term retention, students should study content right before they need to recall it
rows.feedback: Retrieval practice is the act of pulling something out of memory, and studies have consistently shown that this practice does more for long-term retention than rereading or reviewing.
distractors: Reviewing material several times in a row is the most reliable way to commit it to memory
Learning is strongest when students are exposed to information in as many formats as possible
To support long-term retention, students should study content right before they need to recall it
rows.correct: Pulling information from memory strengthens long-term learning more than rereading.

rows.stem: A colleague says, "My final exam is all multiple-choice. What's the best way for my students to practice?" Based on the video, what's the strongest answer?
rows.correct_blob: Have them practice with multiple-choice questions.
rows.distractors_blob:
Have them practice with open-ended essay questions ||
Have them rewrite their notes multiple times ||
The practice format won't affect their success on the exam
rows.feedback: The key idea is that the format you practice in should match the format you'll be tested in. Essays and rereading have their place, but for an exam that is fully or largely multiple choice, practicing with multiple-choice questions should be part of the preparation process.
distractors: Have them practice with open-ended essay questions
Have them rewrite their notes multiple times
The practice format won't affect their success on the exam
rows.correct: Have them practice with multiple-choice questions.

rows.body:
The rest of this module will focus on using AI, specifically AI chatbots, to support the writing of multiple-choice questions.

There are a few basic concepts you should know before continuing:

-- AI chatbot
-- Copying, pasting, and the clipboard

If you aren't confident about any of these concepts, you can use the Quick Start Guide below to receive the basic information you need before you proceed.

rows.stem: The video described several problems that commonly show up when AI writes multiple-choice questions. Select all of the problems it mentioned.
rows.correct_blob:
The correct option is often longer than the others ||
The distractors are too implausible to be effective ||
The question is pitched at the wrong cognitive level ||
The AI falls into a rut, writing the same kind of question over and over
rows.distractors_blob:
The stem is too detailed, incorporating a lot of extraneous details ||
The question contains 5 choices, instead of 4 as requested
rows.feedback: Although there are many potential issues with using AI to write exam questions, these four are the ones I chose to mention because they are the most common ones I've personally encountered.
distractors: The stem is too detailed, incorporating a lot of extraneous details
The question contains 5 choices, instead of 4 as requested
rows.correct:
The correct option is often longer than the others ||
The distractors are too implausible to be effective ||
The question is pitched at the wrong cognitive level ||
The AI falls into a rut, writing the same kind of question over and over

rows.body: Now let's look at the question-writing app. You will see me demonstrate how to target a particular course and topic for the questions I want it to create.

rows.stem: In the app's workflow, how do the app and your AI chatbot interact?
rows.correct_blob: The app copies the prompts onto your clipboard, and you must paste them into the AI chatbot
rows.distractors_blob:
The app sends your questions directly to the AI, but it can not see the AI's responses ||
The AI chatbot controls the app, selecting and using the prompts it judges to be the most useful ||
The app will show you the prompt, and it is your responsibility to type them into the AI chatbot
rows.feedback: This is a key aspect to understand: the moment you click a button for a prompt, it will copy that prompt onto your computer's clipboard, and it is then up to you to paste it into your AI chatbot. You are always free to modify the prompts before sending them, or to type in your own prompts, but using the ready-made prompts from the app will save you time.
distractors: The app sends your questions directly to the AI, but it can not see the AI's responses
The AI chatbot controls the app, selecting and using the prompts it judges to be the most useful
The app will show you the prompt, and it is your responsibility to type them into the AI chatbot
rows.correct: The app copies the prompts onto your clipboard, and you must paste them into the AI chatbot

rows.stem: The app's three main question-level tools each do a different job. Match each button to what it does.
rows.correct_blob:
Generate Alternatives::Offers several different versions of the whole question to choose from
Refine Correct Answer::Generates alternate versions of the correct answer
Refine Distractors::Produces a large set of distractors to pick from
rows.feedback: Those three buttons cover most of the question-level work: *Generate Alternatives* when you want a different take on the whole question, and *Refine Correct Answer* and *Refine Distractors* to replace the options with alternatives that better match your needs.
rows.correct:
Generate Alternatives::Offers several different versions of the whole question to choose from
Refine Correct Answer::Generates alternate versions of the correct answer that match the distractors in length and complexity
Refine Distractors::Produces a large set of distractors to pick more plausible ones from

rows.stem: The video introduced several ways to audit your question set. Match each audit to what it checks.
rows.correct_blob:
Question Type Audit::Classifies accepted questions by nursing practice perspective and suggests changes to improve balance
Difficulty Audit::Classifies each question as Easy, Moderate, or Hard and shows the difficulty distribution of your question set
Bloom's Level Audit::Assigns each question a Bloom's taxonomy level and alerts you to any levels you haven't covered
rows.feedback: The Question Type Audit checks how accepted questions represent different nursing practice perspectives and suggests changes that could improve the balance. The Difficulty Audit groups questions by difficulty, while the Bloom's Level Audit examines the cognitive levels required to answer them.

rows.body:
Open the app in training mode by clicking the link below:

https://jin-dissertation.github.io/dissertation-app/?mode=training

Use your participant code to sign in and keep your AI chatbot open in another tab or window. Spend about 15 minutes trying to create questions on a topic you teach. These are practice goals, not graded requirements:

1. Try to accept at least 5 questions.
2. Try each main question-refinement prompt at least once.
3. Try each audit prompt at least once.

The blue training tips in the app will provide helpful tips. 15 minutes after you begin, the app will alert you and ask you to return to this module. When you're ready, come back here to wrap things up.
If you have any questions or concerns, please email me at tjin@crimson.ua.edu

The findings mentioned in this module come from the following sources:

Birkhead, S., Kelman, G., Zittel, B., & Jatulis, L. (2018). The prevalence of multiple-choice testing in registered nurse licensure-qualifying nursing education programs in New York State. Nursing Education Perspectives, 39(3), 139–144. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.nep.0000000000000280

Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L., III. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science, 319(5865), 966–968. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1152408

Moran, V., Wade, H., Moore, L., Israel, H., & Bultas, M. (2022). Preparedness to write items for nursing education examinations: A national survey of nurse educators. Nurse Educator, 47(2), 63–68. https://doi.org/10.1097/nne.0000000000001102
